# The name Inaras and the world it opens

A name is a door. **Inaras** opens onto an entire world: the domain of wild animals, hunt, a Hittite tradition, and centuries of storytelling, worship, and scholarship. This post walks through that world room by room — the name and its roots, the original script, the sound of it, the myths, the symbols, the sites, the afterlife across cultures — and ends at the newest room of all: a Unicode domain that makes the whole structure addressable. *inaras* gets you to the same building, but only the restored form tells you why it was built.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Inaras
- **ASCII form:** inaras
- **Meaning:** "Unknown"
- **Domain of influence:** Wild Animals, Hunt
- **Pantheon:** Hittite
- **Classification:** Tier 2
- **Original script:** 𒀭𒄿𒈾𒊏 (Cuneiform (Hittite))

## Overview

**Inaras** (*inaras*) — Wild Animals, Hunt · Unknown — belongs to the Hittite tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Wild Animals, Hunt". The name means "Unknown".

**Inaras** is the Hittite goddess of the wild animals and the open steppe. She appears most dramatically in the Myth of Illuyanka, where she persuades a mortal named Ḫupašiya to help her trap the dragon that has defeated the storm-god. Her domain is the untamed country beyond the city: the grazing herds, the swift gazelles, and the dangerous borderlands where civilization meets wilderness.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Inaras** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/inaras/). The restoration needs no distinctive letters or diacritics its ASCII form would lose, which places the name in Tier 2. The plain ASCII form *inaras* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

The name is attested in Cuneiform (Hittite) as **𒀭𒄿𒈾𒊏**. Etymologically it means "Unknown".

The ASCII form *inaras* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Inaras** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The restoration needs no distinctive letters or diacritics its ASCII form would lose, which places the name in Tier 2.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **i** → **I** — Same, capitalized
- **n** → **n** — Same

- **r** → **r** — Same

## The Original Script

The name is preserved in Cuneiform (Hittite) as **𒀭𒄿𒈾𒊏** — Sumero-Akkadian cuneiform (Hittite scribal tradition), attested Hittite Empire, c. 1400–1180 BCE, in Anatolia (Ḫattuša). The script is written left-to-right.

The scholarly transliteration is *ᵈi-na-ra (acc. ᵈi-na-ra-an)* (Hittitological), giving the normalized reading /ˈinara/.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Written ᵈi-na-ra(-an) in the Illuyanka myth (CTH 321)

The name is attested in Hittite cuneiform as **𒄿𒈾𒀸** (i-na-ra-aš). The Unicode restoration **Inaras** gives the scholarly citation form; the ASCII form *inaras* is a domain-name convenience.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/iˈnaːras/** — Hittite Reconstruction.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **I-** — Close front vowel [i], the light first syllable.
- **-na-** — Syllable with nasal [n] and open vowel [a].
- **-ras** — Tapped [r] with open [a] and final sibilant [s].

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: Scholarly reconstruction /iˈnaːras/; the exact ancient pronunciation is debated.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Hittite** — Inaras, goddess of the wild animals and the open steppe
- **Cuneiform** — 𒄿𒈾𒀸 (i-na-ra-aš)
- **Mythic role** — Mistress of animals who traps the dragon Illuyanka with a mortal ally

Inaras is Tier 2: the restored form preserves the scholarly citation shape but adds no distinctive diacritic; the ASCII form is a domain-name convenience; the cuneiform original is written in the Sumero-Akkadian syllabary.

## Mythology

Inaras is best known from a single, brilliant episode, but that episode reveals a goddess of cunning, sovereignty over animals, and alliance between divine and mortal.

### The Feast of the Dragon (Illuyanka myth)

After the storm-god Tarḫunash is defeated by the dragon Illuyanka, Inaras takes action. She prepares an enormous feast of beer, wine, and every kind of food, then goes to the mortal Ḫupašiya and proposes a bargain: if he helps her trap the dragon, she will sleep with him. Ḫupašiya agrees. The dragon and his children eat and drink until they cannot return to their hole, and Ḫupašiya binds them so that Tarḫunash can destroy them.

### Inaras and Ḫupašiya (Mortal alliance)

The myth places a mortal at the center of divine victory. Inaras does not defeat the dragon alone; she enlists human cunning and desire. After the deed she warns Ḫupašiya not to look out the window while she is away, but he disobeys and sees his family. The story ends with the establishment of a ritual in memory of the event.

### Lady of the Steppe (Wild domain)

As goddess of the wild animals, Inaras guarantees the abundance of game and the balance between human hunters and animal herds. Her domain is the dangerous, fertile margin between the settled land of Hatti and the wilderness beyond.

### The Annual Festival (Ritual foundation)

The myth of Illuyanka was not only entertainment; it grounded an annual festival in which the defeat of the dragon was ritually re-enacted. Inaras's cunning was thus remembered every year as the beginning of the storm-god's renewed power.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Inaras concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Gazelle** — The swift animal of the steppe, emblem of her wild domain.
- **Bow and arrow** — The tools of the hunt and the means by which she governs animals.
- **Feast** — The banquet of beer and wine by which Illuyanka is lulled and trapped.
- **Steppe grass** — The open land that is her kingdom.
- **Serpent/dragon** — The enemy she helps to defeat, symbol of chaotic waters.

## Archaeology & Evidence

The texts that name Inaras were excavated from the Hittite royal archives at Boğazköy-Hattusa and related sites in central Anatolia, including temple storerooms and administrative buildings within the citadel. The tablets belong to the corpus of Hittite cuneiform literature preserved in the imperial chancery, with duplicates and parallels in Hurrian, Hattic, Luwian, and other Anatolian traditions. Many were written or copied during the Empire period (c. 1400–1180 BCE), though some compositions may descend from older oral or written sources. The clay tablets were baked, either deliberately or by the fire that destroyed the city, which helped preserve them for modern excavation and study.

## Realm & Domain

**Inaras** is the Hittite goddess of the wild animals and the open steppe. She appears most dramatically in the Myth of Illuyanka, where she persuades a mortal named Ḫupašiya to help her trap the dragon that has defeated the storm-god. Her domain is the untamed country beyond the city: the grazing herds, the swift gazelles, and the dangerous borderlands where civilization meets wilderness.

### Mistress of Animals

She rules the wild herds and the creatures of the steppe.

### The Trap

She devises the feast that lures the dragon Illuyanka to his doom.

### Steppe Wanderer

Her home is the open grassland, not the palace or the temple.

### Divine Huntress

She knows the ways of animals and the arts of the chase.

## Across Cultures

Inaras shares traits with several ancient Mediterranean and Near Eastern figures.

Her role as mistress of animals recalls the Greek Potnia Theron, the Mistress of Animals who presides over wild creatures, and Artemis in her capacity as huntress. The dragon-slaying story has close Indo-European parallels, especially the dragon fight of the storm-god. Inaras's liaison with a mortal helper also resembles stories in which a goddess enlists a human hero. Yet her Hittite form is distinct: she is not a virgin huntress but a sovereign of the steppe who uses sex, food, and cunning as weapons.

Kindred figures in the PuniCodex cross-tradition index include [[anat|ꜥAnat]], [[artemis|Ártemis]], [[fionn|Fionn]], [[hoori|Hoori]], [[ochosi|Ọṣọọsì]], and [[pan|Pān]], each linked through hunt / wild.

## Cultural Legacy

Inaras survives in scholarly memory as the Hittite Mistress of Animals and the architect of the dragon's defeat.

She appears in studies of Indo-European dragon combat, comparative mythology, and the role of goddesses in ancient Near Eastern narrative. The Myth of Illuyanka is one of the most widely cited Hittite texts, and Inaras's role in it makes her a key figure for understanding how divine and mortal agency interact in Hittite thought. For PuniCodex, she represents the wild, cunning dimension of the pantheon: the goddess who knows the borderlands and how to turn an enemy's appetite into his destruction.

## A Meditation

Inaras is the goddess of the edge: the place where the city ends and the steppe begins, where human craft meets animal instinct, and where cunning can defeat strength. Her story warns that even a dragon's power can be undone by appetite, and that the wild is not simply chaos but a realm with its own sovereign.

## A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In the case of **Inaras**, the map does not lead through diacritics or special letters, because the source tradition wrote the name in Cuneiform (Hittite) rather than in the Latin alphabet. The ASCII form *inaras* and the restored form share the same letters; the restoration is a decision about which conventional spelling should serve as the public reference.

That decision is not cosmetic. The original script attestation carries semantic and phonetic information that no romanization can fully reproduce. By fixing one conventional spelling as the canonical domain form, the project prevents the drift that happens when a name is romanized differently in every article, map, and database. The breakdown still lists each character — **i**, **n**, **a**, **r**, **a**, **s** — so visitors can see exactly what is being carried forward and what is not. What looks like "no change" is, in fact, a deliberate choice to keep the name stable, searchable, and addressable.

A domain name is a kind of publication. When **Inaras** resolves, it proves that the restored spelling is not a theoretical exercise; it is a working address on the public internet. Search engines can index it, language models can encounter it, and anyone who copies it from a manuscript can paste it into a browser. That practical reality changes the status of the restoration. ## Restoration Notes

Restoring a name is not a single decision; it is a sequence of smaller decisions, each backed by a different kind of evidence. For **Inaras**, the chain begins with the attested form in Cuneiform (Hittite), continues through the standard scholarly romanizations, and ends with the DNS-compatible Unicode spelling used by this temple. The meaning "Unknown" anchors the name in its semantic field; without that anchor, the marks would float free of the figure they name. The restored form **Inaras** and the ASCII form *inaras* share the same Latin letters; the restoration here is a conventional capitalization rather than a recovery of lost diacritics or special characters. Those adjustments are not arbitrary styling. They follow the tier rule that places Inaras in **Tier 2**: the restoration needs no distinctive letters or diacritics its ASCII form would lose. The rule is mechanical, not editorial, which means the same standard applies to every entry in the lexicon. A visitor who disagrees with the classification can at least see exactly which evidence produced it, because every step is recorded in the Scholarly Edition. That transparency is the difference between a restoration project and a branding exercise. The name is being put back, not invented.
